To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the model can fit the bibliometrics of a token journal, (2) the model can simulate the collective problem solving by scientists, (3) the simulation suggests that cumulative advantage processes do not improve scientists' ability to find good scientific solutions, (4) referring to publications that have passed peer review is important for scientists to find good solutions.

(1) a simulation of the scientific process can reproduce the distribution of citations per paper and papers per author found in the literature, and (2) the simulation shows that citation practices that lead to cumulative advantage in the distribution of citations do not lead to better collective problem solving, while citation practices that only refer to publications that have been peer reviewed do.

(i) cumulative advantage is not a necessary condition for the emergence of scale-free citation distributions, (ii) cumulative advantage is a poor heuristic for collective learning or problem-solving in science, and (iii) the best heuristic for collective learning in science is to refer only to publications that pass peer review.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the micro-level mechanisms of scientific publishing affect collective learning in the sciences.
the relationship between individual and collective learning in science, and the mechanisms by which the two might interact.
the question of how the micro-level practices of scientists can affect the macro-level structure of science.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model is a useful tool to test hypotheses about the relationship between citation practice and collective learning.
citation practice does not affect scientists’ ability to solve scientific problems.
the simulation model is a valuable tool for exploring the dynamics of scientific publication and citation, and for testing hypotheses about how the dynamics affect the collective learning of science.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cumulative advantage in citations does not improve collective learning, but that collective learning can be improved by using peer review to select publications.
a model of science as a network of agents can simulate the collective problem solving of science.
the model shows that citation practice can affect both collective learning and cumulative advantage, but the two effects are independent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cumulative advantage process is not a necessary condition for the collective learning of scientists.
cumulative advantage in the distribution of papers per author does not improve the ability of scientists to find better solutions to their problems.
a model of science can help to distinguish between practices that are good for science, and those that are good for scientists.
